#4000. The Sunday Papers

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

Sundays are for waking up covered in sand. The roof of your house is missing. A small man stands in the emptied bed of a dump truck. "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6," he says. "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6," he repeats. "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6," he declares once again, beginning to move towards you this time. "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6." You realise your hands are tied down. Oh no.

Is he about to sit on your face? WAIT, THAT'S NOW ILLEGAL HERE IN THE UK. NO, PLEASE, DON'T SIT ON MY-time seems to slow as the bare backside approaches your visage. As its cheeks prepare to become as sandy as yours, you hear its wielder say: "And we thought, hey, given the moment..."

Panicking, you scrabble for anything to say which might free you before something that might get a British MP's hackles up can occur. "Things first went awry when I turned up for my appointment to find a tall German man wearing a cowboy hat asking a PR if he could play the game," you blurt out. The posterior momentarily stops moving towards you. Buoyed, you continue to tell a story you heard from VGC's Chris Scullion.

I was asked if I minded sharing my one-to-one appointment with this chap too, to which my inherent British cowardly courtesy kicked in and I lied that it was perfectly fine.

"I want drums", he said as he entered the room. "We are playing Dani California by Red Hot Chili Peppers." Rather than ask him whether he also fancied telling me where I was going for dinner later, I picked up my guitar and went along with it, eager to just play the game.

The bottom begins its agonising crawl towards your kisser once more. You can feel the occupants of parliamentary benches begin to sense a disturbance in the force. Maybe if you can make the bumholder sad, that'll do the trick. You try to remember how Sebastian Cardoso of Game Studio Unlocked's presentation on the tragic fates of game studios after acquisitions went.

A hundred and twenty-three of the 362 developers were shut outright. The average life from acquisition to closure is 6.4 years and the median is 5, meaning half of all closed studios were dead within five years of their acquisition.

The familiar names mostly died fast. EA closed Pandemic two years after buying it. Sony shut Firewalk barely a year and a half in. Warner Bros. closed Player First roughly seven months after acquiring it. Bluepoint, closed at the five-year mark, is exactly what the median looks like.

It's no use. That arse's shadow its creeping across ever more of your face like your're a planet with a nose and it's the Vogon Constructor Fleet. Maybe you can somehow contort your head to the side. Arrrggghh. You call on all the strength of muscles you barely ever use and think of the incredible gymnastic feats executed by Physical Contortion Gamer's Josh Wolens during an ongoing GTA diary series.

Attempting to do flips, then, just sort of rotates your entire body below the diaphragm while your head and chest area remain bolt upright, rigid in such a way that you could feasibly fly a flag from your own thorax.

Which looks odd. Nevertheless, it is pretty fun to scoot and roll your way through Los Santos. At one point, I attempted a double frontflip in the middle of a part of the map that had been deleted for some reason. It didn't quite work out, and I ended up colliding with and possibly killing a man in a fursuit.

It doesn't work. You can't get away. You begin to scream. The posterioperator stops repeating the words "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6". Instead, he asks where that mysterious German cowboy you mentioned earlier has gone. You don't have a clue, and can't help admitting as much. "Ah well." The derriere resumes its descent, now mere inches from your mug. This is the end. You have one last rummage through your mind for possible solutions.

Respec's Tom Orry hasn't managed to save you. "Fine, sit on my face and send me to hell," you shout into the pinkish ring of doom as British cops prepare to ram-raid your abode and arrest you for crimes against a prude's definition of acceptable shagging.

The bum stops. Its owner asks if you've just said the word Sentinel. "Yes," you lie.

The arse is raised and swapped for the face of a man. "What a perfect time for you to realise what The Elder Scrolls 6 is actually called," he says.

You notice he's not Todd Howard. Or Adrian Edmondson.

"It's Ade's month off and they needed another baldy to play this esteemed role," Sir Patrick Stewart announces, clearly responding the look of befuddlement your face can still have since it hasn't been crushed by a ten-tonne tush. You wonder how you didn't recognise his voice before, especially given he played the emperor in Oblivion.

"Here's to the next Bethesda game after Starfield," the Stew sings as the police bust through the door and he's beamed up before they can tackle him.

#3999. Ahead of The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past, here's a "lore friendly unofficial expansion to Geralt's life in Toussaint" from a well-established quest modder

While its remastered upgrade might have broken cover in late September, The Witcher 3's extra expansion isn't set to join it until next year. With 2027 still a month and a bit away, a modder's taken it upon themselves to add a few more adventures to Geralt's time in Toussaint, Blood and Wine's gorgeous French-ish duchy, before the bloke from the river heads off to Letten for Songs of the Past.

So far, only the opening chapter of the mod - Annals of the Duchy - has been released. It adds in a new quest about Geralt, with help from either Yen or Triss if either have made the trip out to Toussaint as part of your playthrough, getting into a scrape thanks to a halfling who seems to promise Gerry the chance to juice up his vineyard's vines.

The mod's creator, Jontej, has previously put together a couple of other custom Witcher 3 quests. While they do look to have used AI voices in English versions of those mods, for Annals of the Duchy they've enlisted a cast of human actors for both Enlish and Polish versions.

Jontej has plans to expand this new questline going forwards, having cited specific "plans for an extra storyline involving Syanna", whom you might remember from Blood and Wine's main quest. Given that - spoilers ahead - the mod relies on you having gotten the Blood and Wine ending which sees both Anna Henrietta and Syanna survive, as well as having paid to renovate the gardens of Geralt's vineyard. They add that, when it comes to their additions, the "timeline fits quite well [with] the upcoming official Songs of the Past Expansion, which has been confirmed to take place after the events of the main game/Blood and Wine".

As much as I've argued that, as of right now, I struggle to see how Songs of the Past will manage to outdo Blood and Wine as a satisfying end to Geralt's tale in the Witcher game trilogy, I am intrigued by the idea of a few more modded adventures showing Gerry adjusting to the semi-retired life. After all, Toussaint's got to have a few more dungeons tucked away that're worth temporarily dusting off the White Wolf's twin swords for.

To kick off Annals of the Duchy, you'll need to trigger its first quest by taking a stroll from the Corvo Bianco manor house down to its gardens between 11am and 1pm. It's worth noting that any other mod which messes with Yen, Triss or companions in general has a chance to muck things up as far as Jontej's creation goes.

#3998. Mass Effect petition has enough signatures for the Canadian Government to potentially save BioWare

Following news of EA's decision to shut down iconic RPG studio BioWare, Canadian fans of the studio have escalated their grievances to the governmental level, calling on the Canadian Government to step in and save the Canadian studio from closure, seemingly after Canada's New Democratic Party leader Avi Lewis called on the government to do so.

Fans have submitted a petition to the Canadian House of Commons arguing for the government to find a way for BioWare to continue, such as through funding that allows the studio to buy the Mass Effect and other IPs and go independent.

The petition, number e-7898, argues that "BioWare is one of Canada's most important cultural exports" and that the studio's closure by its American parent company "represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy."

"BioWare's productions champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights that are at the centre of Canada's national identity," it continued.

The petition opened for signatures on 4th of November, and has already amassed 1,700 signatures. By law, petitions that surpass 500 valid signatures from Canadian citizens or residents are entered into the House of Commons' agenda, meaning they will be presented in front of the parliament.

As encouraging as that may be, it's worth keeping in mind that it may not result in meaningful change. Even if the Canadian Government agrees with the petition's goals, it cannot force EA to sell BioWare or its various IPs.

EA notably didn't shop the studio around before closing it down, and the publisher has a history of closing down owned studios rather than selling them off. EA has also kept the IPs of its various shuttered studios.

The community's reaction to BioWare's closure has taken different forms. Hundreds of thousands signed a different petition to save Mass Effect. The people behind the movement have purchased billboards in Times Square in New York City to advertise it, with plans for more outside The Game Awards ceremony in December.

Meanwhile, former BioWare developers have spoken about the last days of BioWare, and the work they've poured into Mass Effect Universe, the studio's final project before it was shuttered.

#3997. 'We've Heard You!' - Star Wars Galactic Racer Is Officially Adding Split-Screen Multiplayer

An incredible addition to an incredible game

Star Wars Galactic Racer is my favourite game of the year so far. It's an incredible racing title that even surpasses the original Star Wars Episode 1 Racer in my view, and I've had so much fun with the campaign and online multiplayer.

There's just one downside that everyone's been pointing out since it was revealed, and that's the absence of local split-screen multiplayer. With that in mind, the development team have found a way to implement it in a new update.

The update isn't available yet, but will be coming to the game in early 2027. Alongside it will be a new mode called Free Play, which is where you'll be able to freely choose your vehicle, character, planet and race track.

"We’ve heard you! Local split-screen multiplayer racing is coming in early 2027. A dedicated team at Fuse Games has been working hard to bring a brand new mode, Free Play, to STAR WARS: Galactic Racer. This new mode will allow you to choose your vehicle, character, planet, and race track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local split-screen action."

It seems Free Play is the only place where you'll be able to access local split-screen multiplayer in Star Wars Galactic Racer, but that's no surprise considering how solo-focused the main campaign is. They'd literally have to rewrite massive portions of the campaign if they were going to implement split-screen into it.

Anyway, this is just an amazing bonus on top of an already amazing game, and I encourage you to check it out if you enjoy a title like Burnout 3: Takedown - it's fast-paced and frantic, has the same kind of takedown system that you'll remember from that game, and the roguelite campaign is really well designed (online is great fun as well).

If you've played it, let us know what you think of the game in the poll down below!

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch is more worried about screen time

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The UK's Conservative Party leader, Kemi Badenoch, has spoken out about GTA 6 and the inevitable, apparently timeless concerns about video games causing violence, saying she's less worried about that than about children not touching grass.

Speaking in a news conference today (via Sky News), Badenoch is asked about how she'd convince parents to reduce screen time for children playing GTA 6, and if she has any concern about "the impact [it] might have on young boys when during the game you might have to shoot civilians and so on."

The Tory leader has more concern about one of these things than the other. "I think I'd be more worried about the amount of time people were spending on a game than the game specifically," she begins. "I remember in my childhood playing Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter – I didn't hit anybody after playing those games.

"I haven't played Grand Theft Auto," she continues, while acknowledging that "I know people are worried about the game content." Badenoch adds: "I'd be more worried about a kid who is in their bedroom all day, who played it all day, than one who spends half an hour on it and then went out and did something else."

Gamers have been dealing with the suggestion that games can inspire violence for decades now, and it's little wonder that GTA 6 is bringing that conversation back up in one form or another. Before Miami-Dade's slew of real-life marketing kicked off earlier this year, Republican Miami-Dade County commissioner Juan Carlos Bermudez and Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz both spoke out against the concept, with Bermudez saying that "we should be promoting the Miami-Dade we have worked so hard to build, not a fictional version of our community defined by crime and violence."

He said he was "not against video games, but to go out and get a video game where – which glorifies not only our first responders getting shot, but also pedestrians and residents – it's nonsensical."

Anyway, since then, a $1 million billboard went up in Miami, and the Miami Heat is being turned into the Vice City Heat for a special game this week, so that argument clearly wasn't particularly effective.

#3995. Mega Man: Dual Override's Boss Design Contest Winner Has Been Decided

Publisher Capcom has revealed the winning robot master in its design competition for Mega Man: Dual Override.

From a shortlist of six finalist designs, the development team chose Cleanser Man as the winner, and it has been made into one of the action platformer's eight boss characters.

Director Shinya Ikuta and Producer Hiroyuki Minamitani make the announcement in the above video, where Cleanser Man's in-game appearance makes its debut.

They thank all entrants for taking part, and talk a little bit about why the character was chosen to appear in the upcoming game.

A new message on the official website provides slightly more detail on what Capcom liked about Cleanser Man:

"It wasn't easy picking a winner, but we ended up deciding on Cleanser Man due to his whimsical motif and unique color pattern. The lid part on the detergent has a very Mega Man-esque design to it, and we like that the detergent itself is very colorful as well. You have to be careful not to introduce too many elements to prevent the design from becoming too cluttered, so we like that the artist kept things relatively simple. But there's still enough detail to it to give it that genuine Mega Man feel."

The competition has been running for nearly a full year, during which time thousands of contestants submitted their original artwork and Capcom narrowed it down to just a handful of finalists. Ultimately, artist @iregyuradabii took the win.

Cleanser Man is now the fifth robot master to be announced for Dual Override, with another three to go.

#3994. Rockstar were "definitely" thinking about giving a Japanese studio the keys to GTA, says former tech director - "I have a name, but I'm not gonna say it"

Obbe Vermeij on ancient plans for a GTA Tokyo

Since time immemorial, North American and European publishers have racked their brains over ways to make their games sell in Japan, ancient heartland of mythical beings like Mario, Sonic, and Polaroid Pete. In the late noughties, Microsoft launched a big push to give Japanese youth the Xbox virus with such targeted console exclusives as Blue Dragon and Lost Odyssey. And Rockstar once dreamed of making a Grand Theft Auto game set in Tokyo.

Speaking to me last week, Rockstar North's former technical director Obbe Vermeij shared a little about the abandoned project. Emphasis on the "little" – it doesn't appear to have gotten very far, despite recently unearthed allusions to "Tokyo PS2" in GTA 5's source code.

Rockstar's parent company Take-Two Interactive filed a trademark for GTA Tokyo back in 2003, the year before the release of the Los Angeles-flavoured GTA: San Andreas. At the time, Rockstar were apparently looking at collaborating with a Japanese studio on the project. "So this was kind above my pay grade," Vermeij told me. "But yeah, there were negotiations with studios, and I have a name, but I'm not gonna say it, because then it becomes like a bigger thing than it is, and I'll probably get it wrong, and I don't know how far the negotiations were, how serious it was. I mean, it was definitely serious. It was the plan. But I don't know how close it got to actually happening."

The game itself would likely have been a contemporary story, not a historical yarn like Rockstar's subsequent Red Dead Redemption. "It definitely had samurai swords in it, I remember that, but I think it was present-day probably," Vermeij went on. "Or sort of not too [far off] - it wasn't, like, sort of the medieval era in Japanese history, or anything. It was definitely not like that."

Vermeij was at Rockstar from 1995 to 2009, where he worked on the first four mainline 3D GTA games, plus some handheld spin-offs. During that time, he says, Rockstar frequently considered the idea of a Grand Theft Auto set outside the United States. "In the same way that we were always thinking about other games, we also thought about cities that would be cool, and it was always the same list," he said. "It was Moscow, London. Istanbul, Rio de Janeiro, maybe Paris and Tokyo. It was always the same ones that people suggested."

Grand Theft Auto has never quite the money-spinner in Japan that it is in North America and Europe. Localised editions of the original three 3D GTA games were published by Capcom, sometime after the original releases, selling a few hundred thousand copies apiece in their launch years.

"I think perhaps [Rockstar's co-founders] the Housers were a little annoyed that GTA wasn't as big in Japan as they thought it deserved to be," Vermeij reflected. "So it kind of made sense to get a local studio to do it. Japanese people actually kind of like different games from westerners a fair bit. For instance, they don't like first person shooters and stuff. So, it made sense to have a Japanese studio have a shot at it, and I think it would have been really cool, because you know, a GTA made by somebody else in Japanese culture – that's something I would probably play."

Take-Two ultimately abandoned their original "GTA Tokyo" trademark in 2008. It's not clear how much Rockstar have considered setting GTA overseas since Vermeij's day, but co-founder Dan Houser (who left the company in 2020) recently told podcaster Lex Fridman that they ultimately decided it wasn't a credible objective.

“We made a little thing in London 26 years ago - GTA London - for the top-down for PS1," he said. "That was pretty cute and fun, as the first mission pack ever for PlayStation 1. I think for a full GTA game, we always decided there was so much Americana inherent in the IP, it would be really hard to make it work in London or anywhere else. You know, you needed guns, you needed these larger-than-life characters. It just felt like the game was so much about America, possibly from an outsider's perspective. But that was so much about what the thing was that it wouldn't really have worked in the same way elsewhere.”

If this article has left you pining for the Shibuya Scramble NPC-tipping sim that will never be, I bring good news: Japanese developers are quite capable of making their own urban open worlders. The obvious go-tos are Sega's Yakuza/Like A Dragon games, with their abundance of lovingly modelled eateries and discount stores. There's also Ghostwire: Tokyo, a respectable first-person parkour sim, though this particular incarnation of Tokyo has a lot of paranormal congestion. All these games have the advantage of being playable on PC right now. As for GTA 6? Who can say, but Vermeij thinks Rockstar might want to port it sooner to get ahead of the slopcomp craze.

#3993. World of Warcraft: Forever's seemingly stellar launch continues as it soars to the top of Twitch's most viewed games, beating out the likes of League of Legends and Zelda

World of Warcraft: Forever launched last night after a hugely successful beta, and it's not just players getting in on the fun. Blizzard's MMO is also proving quite the attraction for spectators, soaring all the way up to the top of Twitch's most viewed games.

As of writing, World of Warcraft sits at around 385,000 viewers and streamer Ahmpy has the most popular WoW channel, pulling in around 18,300 live viewers.

For comparison, Twitch's ever-popular non-gaming Just Chatting category is the service's second most watched category with 145,000 viewers, and Riot Games' genre-leading MOBA League of Legends takes third place with 81,400 viewers.

Aion 2, another MMO released back in October, is sitting pretty at around 75,900 viewers, while Nintendo's newly released The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake (it's good!) has brought in a wonderful 63,100 watchers on the day of its arrival.

Perhaps contributing to World of Warcraft: Forever's success is the fact it launched with few problems, enjoying one of the smoothest day-one releases in the series' recent history. Its beta proved especially popular, with Blizzard developers calling it one of the most successful betas they've ever seen. One wonders how many of these current Twitch viewers are adults getting their WoW fix during work while their boss isn't looking?

It's official. Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond. After years of speculation and months of final screen tests, it's been confirmed that The Batman star will take on the iconic role.

His first appearance will be in Bond 26, directed by Dune helmer Denis Villeneuve. No date has been set for that yet, but it's likely a few years away yet. But, courtesy of the James Bond Twitter account, we have a first look at Pattinson as Bond.

Identity Confirmed https://t.co/FCU5A9c1wkNovember 16, 2026

Pattinson joins the long line of James Bond stars, played previously by Sean Connery, David Niven, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig. The latter left the role after 2021's No Time to Die, meaning it's been five years of speculation about who could play the part.

The final round of auditions for 007 were reportedly between Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Robert Pattinson, and Nicholas Hoult. Pattinson and Hoult were apparently last minute additions to the screen tests after Amazon MGM Studios were split on the decision for the role.

Now it's been cast, everything is moving full speed ahead towards Bond 26. It's a responsibility that Villeneuve has said he is taking very seriously. "We can't f*** it up," he told GQ recently. "The truth is, we do not have the choice. We have to succeed. We have to honor the legacy, we have to honor the tradition, and there's a ton of Bond fans out there – I'm one of them – and I want this movie to be good, and I will work very hard to make sure we honor that responsibility."

All eyes will be on the return of 007 too as this will mark the first film in the franchise released under Amazon's new ownership and will be the first movie produced under Heyman Films and Pascal Pictures, overseen by David Heyman and Amy Pascal.

#3991. "There is no excuse for what I did," Nvidia CEO says, as affair with an alleged Chinese spy makes the US-China AI race look even more ridiculous

Just saying, Jensen, this probably doesn't happen if you stick to gaming GPUs

Ostensible graphics card company and definite AI giants Nvidia have commissioned an independent investigation into themselves, amid reports that CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Per both the New York Times and Nvidia themselves, Nvidia offered to go under the microscope after US intelligence organisations elected to investigate Huang’s paramour, Chinese national Alice Huang (no, uh, relation, and also known as Huang Le), on suspicion of sharing sensitive information with Beijing. The Nvidia-running, leather-jacketed Huang has thus far only copped to an unspecified affair, admitting in an extraordinary public statement that he was "unfaithful to my wife." Still, the two investigations are likely to start a bizarre new leg in the alread-messy AI arms race that the US and China have been indulging in for years.

See, the basis for Huang and Huang’s relationship appears to be the same thing that’s been fucking us as PC owners: data centres and AI hardware. Alice Huang is a former managing director of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company who’ve bought billions of US dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips – and have been investigated for allegedly getting some of them into the hands of Chinese companies, in defiance of US trade restrictions on goods that might threaten the States’ AI dominance. Possibly also, given both countries’ increasing interest in the technology’s military uses, their perception of national security.

Many of these embargo-dodging accusations originate from after Alice Huang left Megaspeed, though she is now under that separate investigation for intelligence-sharing, and the prospect of any high-tech pillow talk from the lips of someone like Jensen Huang would be very disturbing to the feds indeed. Both Nvidia and their "deeply sorry" CEO deny that he shared sensitive information beyond that required for routine customer/client discussions.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the company’s statement reads. "Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate."

In the US-Sino battle of artificial intelligence, Jensen Huang has – as with his marriage – played both sides. He’s undoubtedly been a, perhaps the driving force behind reinventing Nvidia from beloved makers of gaming gear to the US’ number-one purveyors of environment-ruining, brain-polluting slop technology. But after the Biden administration banned American-made GPU exports to China over fears they’d be used to boost the latter’s military capabilities, Huang successfully lobbied Donald Trump into relaxing those restrictions, allowing Nvidia to flog their wares – including their crème de la crème AI GPU, the H200 – to cash-rich Chinese companies.

In a further twist, many of those chips have got mysteriously stuck in Hong Kong import facilities, suggesting the Chinese government in fact wants AI companies to stick to Chinese-made parts. But then, the Hangzhou-based DeepSeek reportedly trained their latest AI model on illicitly-gained Nvidia tech, so there’s either a healthy black market in operation, or the CCP is willing to tolerate the occasional bit of decadent Western silicone if it helps them catch up to the burger-chomping likes of ChatGPT and Claude. Maybe both, and either way, one can see how a well-placed honeypot could prove useful. Allegedly.

Without wanting to pick sides, in a race where I hope both teams lose, it’s also China who have more work to do. The People’s Republic produces a greater proportion of successful 'open' AI models, where the inner workings and even source code is made public, and mines more of the crucial minerals needed to build components and infrastructure. However, US-produced 'closed' models dominate global AI usage, and despite the lack of minerals, its existing data centres are estimated to wield 40 times the combined compute power of China’s. Probably because they just get all the RAM they need from Best Buy instead of digging it up themselves.

#3990. Nintendo says it isn't planning any more Switch 2 price hikes

Nintendo, which unveiled the results of the first half of its fiscal year 2027 earlier today, has now said it has access to enough quantities of memory to manufacture more Switch 2 consoles.

As a result, the platform holder does not plan to increase the price of the Switch 2. That's according to Reuters, citing Nintendo president Shuntaro Furukawa.

Nintendo, which has so far sold 26m Switch 2 consoles, has already raised the price of the console earlier this year. The price hikes, which took effect on 1st September in the US, Canada, Japan and Europe, saw the console's price increase by $50 / €30 / ¥10,000. Although that was technically the first price hike for the console itself, prior to the Switch 2's launch last year, Nintendo raised the price of Switch 2 accessories in the US as a result of the Trump Administration's tariffs.

The reason that would cause Nintendo to raise prices again is the same that already caused rival PlayStation and Xbox to do so: AI-driven, global memory and storage shortages.

PlayStation already raised PS5 and PS5 Pro prices, on several occasions. Xbox has likewise gone through multiple rounds of price hikes for its Series X and Series S consoles, with the most recent having taken place in August.

That same crisis pushed one of Nintendo's longtime ROM suppliers to exit the business, opting instead to focus on the more lucrative business segments. ROM memory is used in Switch cartridges, though Nintendo hasn't commented on the news.

Incidentally, Switch 2 hardware sales have been in decline for several quarters now compared to its banner launch in 2025. Still, Switch 2 sales are tracking ahead of the Switch 1.

#3989. Poll: What Do You Think The Metacritic Score Will Be For GTA 6?

Considering we're just a few days away from the release of GTA 6 on November 19th, we're bound to start getting reviews at some point between now and launch, and it'll be fascinating to see what the critics think of it!

This is a series that has consistently dominated on Metacritic over the years - a website that takes loads of professional reviews and creates an average score based around them. Grand Theft Auto V has a 97 average rating on there, for example, while GTA 4 goes even higher with a 98 rating.

In fact, every mainline release since GTA 3 (not including stuff like Chinatown Wars and Liberty City Stories) has reached at least a 95 on the platform. To put that into context, the best-rated Xbox Series X game of the year on Metacritic right now is Hades 2, and that game has a 95 average rating.

Feature These Are Xbox's Best 25 Games From 2001-2026 According To Metacritic

If we're going off history alone, GTA 6 has every chance of becoming the highest-reviewed game of 2026 on Xbox and PS5. The question is whether it'll manage to hit those highs once again, or whether it'll struggle to meet the hype.

Let's not forget there's never been a wait like this for a GTA game before, and while absence definitely does make the heart grow fonder, it also creates a sense of expectation that's extremely difficult to live up to.

We'll have to wait and see what happens! You'll find a review roundup on Pure Xbox ASAP, and it seems the smart bet is at least a 95 rating on Metacritic, although that's much easier said than achieved.

#3988. PlayStation Black Friday Sale Is Live Now, Up to $100 Off PS5 Accessories, PSVR2

Update [Mon 16th Nov 2026, 1pm]: The range of Black Friday sales and offers from PlayStation are live now, allowing you access to the discounts below. Here's a link to the PlayStation Direct sale, which is where you'll find the vast majority of the sales.

As a reminder, most discounts will be available until 30th November, but the discounted controllers extend into December.

Original Story: Alongside its ongoing PS Store Black Friday sale and a new PS Plus promotion that goes live tomorrow, Sony has also detailed the range of discounts it'll apply to PS5 accessories from 16th November 2026.

Here are the discounts Sony is offering on PlayStation Direct and at participating retailers:

If you're a PS Plus member from Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, or the United Kingdom, then you can save an additional 5% on the sale price if you order through PlayStation Direct.

There shall also be discounts for physical copies of Marvel's Wolverine, Saros, Ghost of Yotei Complete Edition, Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls, and more.

News PS Plus Subscriptions on Sale Now, But There's a Big Catch

Feature 80+ PS5, PS4 Games to Buy in PS Store's Updated Black Friday Sale

PS5 and PS4 games going cheap we recommend

Of course, what you won't find in the list of Black Friday discounts is any offers relating to the base PS5 console or the PS5 Pro. Neither machine is going on sale during Black Friday this year. That marks a change compared to last year's promotion, where Sony had a new PS5 bundle featuring Fortnite to sell at a $100 discount. No such thing appears to exist this year.

Since we are now just days away from GTA 6 launching, and with these discounts going live tomorrow for two weeks, I can't say I'm too surprised — Sony will know it can sell PS5 consoles at full price with the Rockstar title looming.

Will you take advantage of any of these imminent PS5 offers? Let us know in the comments below.

Both PSVR2 + PS5 Pro & Quest 3 compliment one another. Yet their blemishes are becoming that much more noticeable at this point. PSVR2's lenses(Fresnel, plus they there's a diffusion layer applied to mitgate screen door effect), PenTile OLED(Mura & less clear image vs RGB), just 18 PPD, god rays, glare, Chromatic Abberation, and form factor are all showing their age.

Quest 3 corrects all of that, as it has clarity in the bag, but then you have to deal with lousy black levels(LCD display), weaker 3D depth perception(Lower stereo overlap), no DFR, Weak stand alone power and no display port for PCVR. They're both in an awkward position for me in 2026. And Steam Frame? If it had display port, a QD Mini-LED or MicroOLED and higher stereo overlap, I'd bite. But as is, it's too expensive for what it's giving.

@CaptD Get on it dude! Hell, It's worth buying just to experience Resident Evil Village(Especially), RE4 VR, including Subside + Makoa Shelf. The latter is the perfect PSVR2 showcase with PS5 Pro. It's pushing the headset & PS5 Pro to it's limits, and at 90fps. Meanwhile, the VR cutscenes in RE Village are jaw dropping stuff.

Unfortunately, Village & 4 run at 60fps with reprojection, so you'll have to deal with that annoying motion duplication-effect. Then you've got MADiSON(Good luck! it's the most terrifying piece of entertainment you'll ever experience), Propogation Hotel(For Resident Evil fans), Compound(Brilliant VR boomer shooter) and more.

And I couldn't for the life of me enjoy Village on my 65" OLED TV. Funny how I get zero motion sickness playing it in VR, but on my TV it makes me queezy and that's because of OLED sample & hold motion blur. There's nothing natural about playing it on a TV since there' zero S3D depth percetion, everything is small scale, the motion clarity is blurry(DrunkOvision), you can't properly get a gage or differentiate the positioning or distance from objects, walls etc because it's essentially a near flat image in motion. in VR? Absolutely! It feels natural to the eyes, minus the odd motion doubling.

Blur free motion clarity & Stereoscopic 3D are the two big missing puzzles to the modern 4K TV puzzle. I don't think we'll get there until the 2030's. Until then, we've got Meta VR Glasses and it's microOLED display, higher resolution(etc) with that can practically get the job done for games using a Virtual Screen. S3D & VR? Check, CRT-tier motion quality? Damn near close. Too bad it has a meesily 70d FOV. Not ideal at all for VR games, but it should be fine with Virtual Screen based titles and 3D movies.

@XLR80Z VR is amazing. It's been transformative, ever since 2016. Once you experience the good stuff it'll feel like you've experienced gaming for the first time all over again. and if it weren't PSVR2 i doubt I'd be playing my PS5 all that much. The veil has been lifted, and it's hard going back to specific genre's on a TV these days. Because i just sit back and think how it would all go down in first person, 3rd person, top down, SideScroller(etc) in VR, be it traditional controls or motion based.

I'm in that funky position where I love Retro(80's & early 90's gaming), and NewWave retro(Think Blazing Chrome, Curse of the Moon, Cuphead etc), including some of Nintendo & Capcoms modern exclusives. But for practically everything else, it's just starting to feel a bit samey & kind of played out. I've been gaming since the later 80's, and I want something that will truly blow me away. That doesn't exist with consoles anymore, since we've enterted the land of graphical diminishing returns. Any level of wow factor all resides in VR imo.

VR is the reason why I'm struggling to get into RE: Requiem on my 65" OLED. it feels like nothing now. Zero scale, no depth, suspense gets dialed down dramatically, that visceral feeling is completely vaccant, the scares don't land compared to how they do in VR, there's no zero wow factor. It's just a flat near depthless screen in motion, and as good as it's Gyro aiming is when dialed in properly, it can't compete whatsoever vs using PSVR2's Sense controllers in each as if you're aiming in real life.

I've caught a glimse of the PCVR Requiem Mod using my Quest 3(YouTube VR 180d gameplay footage), and even at just 180d @60fps(PCVR version is in full VR @90fps), it blows the lid off the flatscreen version. On a TV, Requiem feels like just another video game, a great video game, but familiar. Yet in VR it's an experience you'll never forget.

Seeing that tall monstrous creepy female stalker enemy(Whater it's name is) during the beginning of the Care Center as Grace in the PS5/PS5 Pro Reqiuem demo feels like one big whatever, when played on a TV. But with PCVR? Good lord man....Enjoy your weekly nightmares! It's unreal.

I haven't tired of flat screen gaming in this generation. If anything I am playing more games and more diverse genres than ever before because of the libraries on Plus.

I noticed playing Walking Dead: Saints and Sinners (Tourist Edition) in PSVR2 on my Pro that it made a sort of black ring around my perspective narrowing my field? of vision. Is that Mura?

Your list of inspiration is pretty much off the beaten path, many I haven't even heard of. Which one has the most FUN (innovative) gameplay of those?

@EfYI I wish i could share the same enthusiasm as you do for modern flatscreen gaming, but VR has ruined that haha. Although, i'm still head over heels for NewWave Retro stuff(My bread and butter!), and the occasional Nintendo & Capcom exclusive etc.

But i want VR for practically everything else, and PCVR seems like the way to go for now. Imagine ILL in VR, or a 3rd person VR mode for Tomb Raider Legacy of Atlantis using a Duelsense controller with traditional controls to play it. Resident Evil Veronica will have a PCVR mod up and running in no time, probably about a month after it gets released on steam in 2027. So many possibilites, PCVR modders are doing gods work.

And that black ring isn't mura, it's probably 'Vignetting' which creates a dark circular shroud surrounding your vision to prevent motion sickness. You have to turn it off in the settings, and it'll be gone. If that's not what you're talking about, than what you're describing is the 110d FOV limitation. It's like wearing a scubidiver mask in every VR game you play. But with Vignetting on(Which i can't stand personally), it creates an almost thick black shround that surrounds the edges of your FOV.

And i would hightly recommend trying Subside's 'Makoa Shelf' DLC, if you really want to be blown away. And of course, RE Village's VR cutscenes are to die for. Mind blowing stuff, even for a dated budget headset like PSVR2. MADiSON(VR Horror)is another huge recommendation if you have the guts to actually get through it, Propogation parodise Hotel and more. But ya, you can just imagine how much better these games would look on better modern headsets like Dream Air, the upcoming Crystal Pro(ect) on a PC with PS6-tier power(Think 5080, or 5070 Ti)

Oh, and as for Mura. It's basically like looking through a cheese cloth. It's always present, but you really start to notice it in dark/black sections in a game. PSVR2's 'pentile' based OLED display not only does it have Mura, but it's less clear than RGB displays, like Quest 3, Steam Frame's and more, because its sub pixel count is lower. Plus sony used a disfusion layer(anti-SDE filter) to their OLED to try and hide or mitigate it's screen door effect. 🤭

Nobody uses Fresnel Lenses(Softer clarity, tiny sweet spot, color fringing, more glare), or Pentile OLED anymore. It's usually Pancake, with RGB MicroOLED, LCD or sometimes QD Mini-LED. Neither RGB LCD or MicroOLED have mura, and they're clearer. Pimax's RGB QD Mini-LED which is being used has very mild mura, if anything in their upcoming Crystal Pro.

Meanwhile, Quest 3 has clarity in the bag. it's almost like a generation ahead of PSVR2, but it faulters with it's milked out LCD black levels, weaker 3D depth perception, no pcvr display port, no DFR etc.

Thank you for explaining that technical detail to me🙏 To think it is a setting, I was convinced that black binocular view = Mura 😂

#3987. This week in PC games: solve the disappearance of 700 people, build a night market for spirits, and play chess on a board that disobeys physics

I don't know what Edwin's been feeding the Maw in my off week, but when I entered its chambers this morning it had left game releases everywhere. Ceiling, walls, floor, they all glisten with games of every size and genre. Even after I hosed away the ones largely made with the assistance of generative AI, the sifting sieves fitted across the drains held a bounty of interesting releases.

Let's get to it, then, before the Maw wakes up and realises I've nabbed all its spoils.

Well, that was potentially too many games in all, even after striking out a fair few that were on my list when I started writing this round up.

It's a busy week for us in the warehouse. Edwin's putting the finishing touches on a series of features he's been working on for months, I'm getting the RPS 100 ready to go live next week, James is wrangling the advent calendar, Mark is working on a write up of a tasty expansion pack, and the guides team are getting everything in order head of the release of GTA 6 next week. One day we will rest, and it will be lovely. But not this week.

#3986. Rockstar shares 38 new screenshots of Grand Theft Auto 6, showing off Vice City, Jason and Lucia, and much more

Rockstar Games have released 38 new screenshots of Grand Theft Auto 6, ahead of its release later this month.

These screenshots, found on a dedicated launch gallery website Rockstar has created, prompts viewers to scroll down and take in the sights of several high quality in-game screenshots snapshotting all kinds of people, places, and events.

These include, but are not limited to, a DJ set in-action, a man and his pitbull looking tough to the camera, a tattooed man getting his hair done (machine gun on hand), and a daring motorbike escape. However, my personal favourite has got to be a lively shot of a dive bar. A band - seemingly called The Rusty Anchor is playing - and some older ladies appear to be having a friendly chat with an open-shirt-wearing geezer enjoying a beer.

You can find all the new images in an image gallery below. So look through them at your pleasure:

Grand Theft Auto 6 is due to release on the 19th November on PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. A few days prior, Rockstar employees are voting on whether or not they'd like to officially recognise a developer union, as the Rockstar vs IWBG union employment tribunal comes to a close on the eve of GTA 6's release date.

James Wyatt says the book "does that in a wide spectrum of things"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

During New York Comic Con, I sat down with Wizards of the Coast Principal Game Designer James Wyatt to talk about the upcoming D&D: World of Warcraft book. This is the first of the Dungeons & Dragons Universes Beyond expansions, blending the familiar characters and locations of Warcraft with D&D rulesets.

The process of translating Azeroth to one of the best tabletop RPGs was no easy feat, and it became quite clear that the team really pushed their design philosophies in new directions with D&D World of Warcraft. We spoke about the process of bringing Azeroth to life in a whole new way, translating original World of Warcraft Classes like Evoker to D&D, and about the shared experience of tabletop role-playing games.

GamesRadar+: So just walk me through the project, because there's obviously so much you could draw from World of Warcraft. Is the Lich King (pictured on the cover) the main villain here?

James Wyatt, principal game designer: That's just one of many possibilities. So there is this map pack that comes with a digital code to download an Icecrown Citadel adventure. You can take level 16 characters and brave Icecrown Citadel and get all the way up to level 20 by the time you reach the frozen throne. But that's just one of the many ingredients we are providing for your cooking experience.

D&D World of Warcraft is up for pre-order at Amazon now, where you can also pick up a WoW-themed Dungeon Master's Screen and a Map Pack for the Icecrown Citadel adventure.

We lay out the Alliance versus Horde. Here's the Burning Legion, the Dragonflight, the Elemental Lords, the Old Gods, the Scourge, and for each one [...] we talked about how to implement these themes through a 20 level campaign and beyond. In fact, there's an endgame section for each one. So that is sort of like your tasting menu of ingredients you can add into the campaign and mix however you want.

I talked myself into the idea in my last interview of running a campaign that really focuses on the Alliance Horde conflict. Where you've got a mixed group of characters from both factions who are trying to bring that conflict to an end and having diplomacy and clandestine meetings and subterfuge and intrigue. I think that even a D&D player who's not into WoW can find inspiration here and stuff to throw in a campaign and help build your own world.

Dungeons play a huge role in D&D World of Warcraft. What was the process of figuring out how to translate them?

Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+.

We mostly tried to translate the maps as faithfully as we could to how they appear in the game. I spent a lot of time particularly working on Ice Crown Citadel, just having my high level Druid sneaking around invisible to see how all the pieces fit together and what the building looks like inside and everything. A lot of time flying around the top trying to figure it out as well.

But I think of the dungeon presentations here as very similar to what we did with the half page adventures in the Dungeon Master's guide. It's just a little bit of text on the map and here we're refreshing that a little bit. We take the map and we put pins in and say, okay, here's the dungeon bosses. Here are the things we know you're going to do and the rest we give you some description of what's here, the kinds of creatures you might encounter. But really, that's where the chaos and the fun and improvisation are happening. There's a lot of room for players to do the crazy things that players do because we all know that no plan survives contact with the players. So what's going to happen there?

When you're developing stat lines for something like Illidan, what's that process look like? You're balancing for an entirely different format.

I've been using the word paraphrase a lot. It's not translating from one game to another. What does that feel like? What's the sense that it's trying to convey?

[For] the length of time the boss is going to survive, we tried to give them some survivability obviously. And Illidan's Challenge Rating 24, so he's going to be tough for even a level 20 party, but figuring out those iconic abilities are what is going to make this feel like that fight against Illidan in Lost Temple and how we translate that or express that in D&D.

Has everything from WoW been carried over? Have you found a way to work dailies into this, for example?

No, and that's actually one of the things that we talk about in the adventure chapter. There's tons of ideas in WoW that you could easily port over into D&D. But we spell out a couple of things to watch out for because they are different games, and not all of those quests ported over are going to be fun at the tabletop. If you want to wander around The Barrens collecting Zhevra Hooves… no thanks. It's going to take us 20 minutes to kill one Zhevra as opposed to five seconds. That matters. So we talked about avoiding the grind. Having characters' actions make a difference in the world, make a lasting impact on the world, letting them occupy the spotlight and not other characters.

A mount in an MMO is a victory lap. It's the "I did this thing and I've accomplished something major." Is that the thought process with mounts in this, where it's just a reward? Because in D&D, you could just ask, "Can I go buy a horse?" And your DM might be like, "Yeah."

Exactly. That whole aspect of prestige, of accomplishment, is much harder to reproduce in any way in a D&D game. So when you kill the Lich King, he does drop the Rains of Invincible, so you can have that special mount. That's pretty cool.

But yeah, you can also just go and buy a Pandarian Dragon Turtle… So that element is still there. It's just not really in the forefront.

It's not a game of individual achievement. Anything that you did at the table, you did with your friends and so you all shared that glory. Travel speed is not a constant frustration for a D&D player the way it is for an MMO player that you need to overcome.

What do you think is one lesson you learned from this entire experience? What do you think is something that's going to stick with you?

There's a lot of little things in terms of design where I hope my goal is to push the rest of the design team forward on some things that I learned from doing this. I'm really curious about the way we did the Death Knight and the Demon Hunter as what we call a Hero Class using WoW language, a subclass that alters your base features.

There's some interesting potential there that we could use in core D&D as well. I don't know yet what that's going to look like, what classes those might be, no idea, but it's something I want to explore. Pushing our monster design forward similarly, but even little things like the Druid's specific wild shaped forms. We already did this for a future book with a Cataclysm Druid or whatever it's called now where you take on a kaiju form basically. We used the same technology. I pulled out these stat blocks from the draft as it existed then and said this is the model you should follow.

That's what we do as a team. We're constantly pushing our design forward. I think this book does that in a wide spectrum of things. The cool thing about it is it's almost an Everything book with something for everybody here, just focused around Azeroth.

Dungeons & Dragons: World of Warcraft launches on November 17, 2026.

That Cataclysm Druid Wyatt mentions could be a part of the upcoming Dark Sun reboot, which is due to launch early next year.

#3984. "The lesson learned is you can have both": Skyrim lead designer reckons there's merit in Baldur's Gate 3-style tough choices and Bethesda's do-anything approach

How many doors should be open at any point in an adventure?

Whether RPGs are better off prioritising player freedom or endeavouring to have several doors slam shut every time you put another foot forwards in order to encourage multiple runs with different characters is, to put it bluntly, something I reckon will still be a matter of debate in the year 4000. We'll all have evolved in non-corporeal beings floating in a galaxy that's been racked by such change that even the six million copies of The Elder Scrolls 5 we've littered the Earth with will have been swept away into the great recycling bin on the gods' desktop, and there'll still be sniping going on about whether it's ok that Skyrim lets you be a master thiefssassin who leads the companions, knows every spell under the sun, and slapped up a world-eating dragon for fun.

For what it's worth, the game's lead designer reckons both games that do and don't let you do that have their merits when executed well.

Speaking to The Examined Game, ex-Bethesda dev Bruce Nesmith talked about being "pleasantly surprised" when playing Baldur's Gate 3 just how much he enjoyed making "consequential decisions that closed off gameplay". In Nesmith's view, Larian "redefined things in a certain way" with their take on the D&D universe and the fantasy rules it plays by. However, he argued that there's still merit to taking an approach more akin to Bethesda's post-Morrowind Elder Scrolls entries and striving to make it possible for the player to see the majority of what the game has to offer in a single playthrough.

"They were both fun," he said. "They were just fun in different ways and that to me was part of the surprise. I would have expected to fall on one side or the other, as if they were things that you couldn't have both [of]. The lesson learned is you can have both. I can enjoy this game over here that does it this way and enjoy this game over here that does it that way."

Nesmith made clear that he still thinks the idea of, with a few exceptions like Skyrim's civil war, not gating the player off from the likes of doing multiple faction questlines is a "very good philosophy" that he supports.

As much as it's always a bit of a cop out to declare that everything's equally good, actually, I do think that there's merit in both approaches. I love the dedication the likes of New Vegas, Disco Elysium, and The Witcher 2 have to making you pick a path and see where it takes you at the expense of not seeing other stuff. Hell, the latter game's infamous for being totally different depending on who you choose to waltz off with at the end of the opening act.

That said, Skyrim's open-endedness was undoubtedly one of the factors which made it so easy for me to get majorly into when I was just cutting my teeth in RPGs as a teenager. There's value in such games existing, even if for plenty it might be as a gateway drug to games with crunchier and more challenging narratives that do demand you plug in your brain and carefully consider every choice you make. Whether there's still as much value in being the gateway drug nowadays compared to in 2011 is the question The Elder Scrolls 6'll likely answer whenever it rocks up. Coming as it is after the likes of BG3 and The Witcher 3 have had near Skyrim-level gangbusters success while leaning a lot more heavily into the hard stuff typically pegged as having less potential for mass appeal.

For what it's worth, while you can very much argue about the execution, Fallout 4's main quest was a lot more choice-heavy than Fallout 3's. So, Bethesda may well opt to pivot or make compromises in their player freedom-first ways if they feel some crunchier choice is in order.

#3983. Xbox Is Releasing Two First-Party Expansions In December 2026

December is often a very quiet month for new game releases, and that's particularly going to be the case in 2026 due to GTA 6's arrival and the desire from publishers to get as far away from it as possible, but we've still got the likes of Rayman Legends Retold and Stage Tour to look forward to, along with a couple of first-party Xbox expansions.

In terms of first-party stuff, Xbox is initially releasing a paid DLC pack for Minecraft Dungeons 2 on December 1st called The Humblers Awaken. This DLC is included with the Deluxe Edition of the game if you bought it, and it'll be available separately as well.

You can expect "new quests, unexplored environments, colorful cosmetics, and an expanded arsenal of powerful gear" in The Humblers Awaken, while base game players will also be treated to a free update on the same day, adding in new challenges, weapons and armour.

Then, just a day later, Xbox and Obsidian are releasing a first expansion for The Outer Worlds 2, known as Side Effects Guaranteed. This DLC includes a new narrative story (that'll be concluded in the second part next year), a new region of Elysium Valley to explore, new threats, new perks and an increased level cap.

There's also new weapons, armours, outfits, flaws, a new radio station - you get the picture!

Side Effects Guaranteed will cost $14.99 USD when it arrives on December 2nd, or you'll get it included if you bought either the Premium Edition or Premium Upgrade Edition of The Outer Worlds 2.

Perhaps there's a chance we might get even more from Xbox's first-party studios in December, but as mentioned, it's typically a month where the releases die down. In any case, it's nice to see two expansions on the way very soon!

On this page: Xbox Is Releasing Two First-Party Expansions In December 2026

The Sift is in danger! Something ancient is stirring beneath the ground of the new dimension – a threat that has slumbered for ages and is now beginning to wake. Gather your trusty allies, venture deep into unexplored reaches, take on the not-so-happy humblers, and confront the foes behind their rude awakening!

Side Effects Guaranteed is the first chapter of a two-part expansion for The Outer Worlds 2. A distress signal beckons you and your crew of the Incognito to a derelict ship, where you discover the ship’s crew in suspended animation to keep themselves alive, as they’ve been infected with something that causes explosive cell death. The hunt for a cure leads to Elysium Valley, a brand-new region on Eden.

#3982. Microsoft workers accuse company of trying to get customers "addicted" to AI while forcing it on their own staff and making them party to "human rights violations"

Open letter warns of "a cascade of business and ethics risks"

A group of "concerned Microsoft workers" have published an open letter criticising their employer's "speed-at-all-costs" approach to generative AI, which they argue is "harming our customers, colleagues, shareholders, vendors, and the planet". They accuse Microsoft leadership of trying to get people "addicted" to genAI, while making their own staff miserable by mandating AI usage.

Echoing the on-going BDS campaign against Microsoft's Xbox business, the writers contend that Microsoft have become party to "human rights violations" by selling generative AI technology to Israel's military during the latter's invasion of Gaza, which a UN commission has deemed a genocide. They're also critical of Microsoft's contracts with the USA's draconian Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. While seemingly not against generative AI in principle, they're organising against "the AI industry’s trajectory to continue to enrich AI’s powerful few", pointing out that AI companies now account for a terrifying share of the global stock market.

I know about the letter thanks to Vertical Slice, who cite a New York Times report on Microsoft's recent voluntary buyouts, which follow several waves of mass layoffs at a company with a market value of around $4 trillion.

"For many, working at Microsoft has become joyless and demoralizing, with job satisfaction declining around the same time the company accelerated its AI investments," the workers write. "Crushing workloads, threats of AI job replacement and layoffs, constantly shifting business priorities, and re-orgs destabilize our work environment and erode employee trust in leadership."

The letter organisers complain that "workers are forced to use AI in almost every work area, with little to no training and no strategic rationale besides 'speed'," obliging them to spend a lot of time "learning and relearning tools, fixing AI slop, and reworking or rolling back low-quality features". They feel that Microsoft's generative AI strategy is exposing customers "to overreliance, misuse, and physical and mental harm", not least because "our own research shows that AI agents don’t prioritize user safety, and internal planning documents detail how to 'make people addicted' to AI products." If that last part is an actual quote from an internal feature document, then: yeeeeeeesh.

The writers further take issue with Microsoft's investments in data centers for generative AI use, which may use up a lot of water while contributing to carbon emissions (jeopardising Microsoft's older commitments to reducing their carbon footprint). They note that "our Community-First AI Infrastructure plan makes vague financial and job-creation commitments, but doesn’t address greenhouse gas emissions or other damage already being done."

The organisers also call out their employer for becoming "a partner to human rights violations" by licensing generative AI tools to the Israeli military and ICE. "Not only are we risking reputational, financial, and legal damage, we are allowing our AI products to be used against whole communities for mass surveillance, detainment, deportation, and genocide," they write.

Finally, they take a swing at "Microsoft’s participation in circular investment across a handful of AI leaders " - that is, AI companies pouring cash into each other, which naturally creates the risk of several companies biting the dust if one company's fortunes take a tumble. This ouroboros strategy "exposes workers, customers, shareholders, and society to a cascade of business and ethics risks," the writers claim, noting that AI-linked stocks now dominate the S&P 500 index.

The letter writers have a number of demands. They'd like more say over "AI product strategy decisions", and for Microsoft to consider customer feedback and bring different development disciplines together "to help guard against shipping AI-worsened user experiences". They want Microsoft to "offer quality training and empower workers to integrate AI in their workflows without tying AI use to rewards, reprimand or layoffs." They call on the execs to "end unfair AI-driven workforce reductions and agree to worker protections".

Looking beyond Microsoft's walls, the workers argue that "job opportunities from data center investments are mostly temporary" and that "Microsoft must protect all workers, not attempt to avoid the unionized trades in local communities, and ensure a just transition for all impacted workers."

The letter writers call on Microsoft to "expand Responsible AI and Sensitive Use teams and fund programs to communicate potential harms to users". They would like Microsoft to stop selling AI materials to organisations "if they are engaged in violence, mass surveillance, detainment, deportation, or genocide", requesting that Microsoft "transparently share contracts with all governments and their agencies or contractors, including police and armed forces, and immediately terminate any contracts with those directly or indirectly involved in human rights violations."

The letter writers want Microsoft to "reduce financial dependency on OpenAI and other AI partners and provide transparency into all AI investments". In general, they want their bosses to "stop offloading financial risk to workers, vendors, partners, customers, and shareholders through irresponsible investments and relationships." As regards the environment, the workers are demanding that Microsoft "reaffirm our goal to be carbon negative, water positive, and zero waste by 2030". They want Microsoft to cooperate more with environmental regulators, and "to respect local communities by rejecting dirty energy, engaging fairly and transparently, and refusing to build in resource-scarce areas."

It's not clear who, exactly, is behind the letter, or how many others at Microsoft have signed as of writing. I've requested comment from Microsoft, and will update this piece as and when I hear more.

Rockstar's follow-up is a true changing of the times

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new dawn beckons with GTA 6, and players of the previous Grand Theft Auto are planning a goodbye for the industry-defining juggernaut. To celebrate Rockstar's sequel finally arriving, GTA 5 fans are going to have one last ride around Los Santos, in tribute to a game that's refused to slow down for 13 years.

The event is known as The Last Ride, and it'll take place on November 18, the eve of GTA 6's arrival. CraftizyTV is behind the original idea, posting about it on TIkTok. "For a lot of us, this game wasn't just a game, it was years of memories," they say. Players in GTA Online are going to get together and make a final spin through the streets, valleys, and highways of Grand Theft Auto 5's map before jumping into to the next installment.

Rather than causing more chaos, this will be a subdued jaunt by design. There will be no crime or police chases (surely). You'll start at Los Santos International Airport, and route through Del Perro Pier and Paleto Bay to finish on Mount Chiliad for a stunning view.

The idea is to admire the craft of what's been a fixture of many people's lives for well over a decade at this point. YouTuber Dezoh puts it perfectly in the video above. "I was 13 or 14 years old when [GTA 5] came out, I'm now 27," he says, recording himself partaking in his own solo lap of the sunny hills of Los Santos.

There will be many such cases. The whole landscape of streaming, YouTube, and games media has changed drastically since then. GTA 5 is older than Twitch Plays Pokémon, even.

Some are livestreaming their final hours winding through the cross-generational behemoth. As of me writing this, you can catch the immensely popular GTA 5 and GTA Online video creator The Gaming Gorilla knockin' around, enjoying a life-changing game for what'll likely be one of the last times.

It is weird that GTA 6 is finally here. But it's a reminder all things change and move on. Cherish what you have while you have it.

#3980. God of War: Sons of Sparta Out Now on PS4, New Modes for PS5 Too

God of War: Sons of Sparta is now live and available on PS4, and if you buy it for that console, the purchase includes the PS5 version too.

In addition, the previously detailed Hermes and Erebus modes are live on PS5 and PS4 too. You can learn more about them both below.

Original Story: It's now been confirmed God of War: Sons of Sparta, the mostly forgotten Metroidvania game that launched earlier this year, will indeed be ported back to PS4.

Having debuted on PS5 in February, the PS4 version launches next week, on 16th November 2026.

For both current PS5 owners and any new players on PS4, the base title will be supported by two extra modes: Hermes Mode and Erebus Mode.

Hermes Mode is a speedrun challenge featuring a split-based timer and a scoreboard. You automatically unlock the mode by finishing the game, or you can enter the following cheat code on the main menu to access it straight away:

Hermes Mode Code: Up Up Down Down Left Right Left Right L1 R1 Touch Pad

Then there's Erebus Mode, which revolves around both you and the enemy dying from one hit. It's dubbed the "ultimate challenge" for God of War: Sons of Sparta.

When it launched on PS5 following a shadow drop reveal, Sons of Sparta didn't exactly set the world alight. We enjoyed the adventure, awarding it a 7/10 score in our God of War: Sons of Sparta PS5 review.

"It's a mostly successful experiment; the Metroidvania structure works well with the franchise's mechanics, and it looks and sounds the part. However, it takes too long to really come into its own, leaving the early parts of the game feeling a bit lacking compared to the richer experience found later on."

We were one of the few who did, though, as the overall critic rating on Metacritic sits at a 64.

Now on a less powerful system, it's not like a PS4 version can fix any of its problems. At least it gives those people still using a PS4 a chance to play the game.

PlayStation Buttons based on work by VictorPines, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

#3979. Cyberattack on Sega third-party newsletter distributor reportedly sees over two million email addresses leaked, but Sega accounts unaffected

Japanese email distribution firm Arara were the target of the attack

Sega have revealed that over two million email addresses have leaked due to a cyberattack on Japanese email delivery provider Arara, whom the Like A Dragon and Sonic publishers use to distribute newsletters. Sega and Arara are currently busy investigating what happened in the breach, which doesn't appear to have affected the Sega accounts you can use receive in-game rewards and access a calendar which reminds you when it's Kazuma Kiryu's birthday. The companies have urged those who signed up for the affected newsletters to be wary of potential phishing attempts.

According to Automaton, who've translated Sega's official press release about the cyberattack, 2,196,044 email addresses in total were affected. 92,273 of that number were linked to the newsletter distribution.

The company have listed some specific newsletter releases as having been affected, including two exhibition announcements for this year's Tokyo Game Show, the announcement of arcade rhythm game Chunithm Mate's launch, six newsletters about online character lottery service Sega Lucky Kuji Online, the launch of a rhythm game update dubbed Ongeki Re:Fresh Act.2, and the launch of another arcade rhythm game update called Maimai DX MAGiCAL. Number one, that's a lot of rhythm games, and number two, Sega have advised those who opted in and received those newsletters to watch out for fishing emails from people posing as being tied to Sega or Arara.

Sega reportedly confirmed that - as far as the affected emails go - no names, dates of birth, genders, residential addresses, phone numbers, credit card information, and passwords are known to have been leaked. There had also been no reports of cases where the leaked information had been misused as of the time Sega made their announcement. The company have naturally put distributing any further email newsletters through Arara on hold until their investigation's done and plan to reach out to each affected person individually once the full details of the leak have been confirmed.

While data breaches and cyberattacks are nothing new, there have been a fair few recently, with both Street Fighter makers Capcom and Kingdom Come Deliverance 2 devs Warhorse suffering incidents of their own last month.

#3978. Remakes and new games "both have a place in the stable" says Nintendo boss, buoyed by the success of Star Fox and Ocarina of Time

It's been a good year for Nintendo: between Star Fox - the N64 classic with a dazzling facelift on Switch 2 - and the newly-launched and utterly fantastic Ocarina of Time remake, the platform holder is having a good run. And that's before you get to the likes of Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, Mario Tennis Fever or any of the Switch 2 re-releases of first-party Switch games, like Xenoblade Chronicles 3 or Animal Crossing: New Horizons.

As popular as its other games are, though, you have to admit that 2026 has been a banner year for Nintendo's remakes - both Star Fox and Ocarina of Time have commanded plenty of headline-grabbing attention over the past 12 months, and it's a fact that isn't lost on the company. In a new interview with Polygon, Nintendo's Nate Bihldorff - senior vice president of product development and publishing - says that wholly new games and remakes of classics are of "equal importance" to the publisher going forward.

"I do think that new games and remakes both have a place in the Nintendo stable, of equal importance to be honest," Bihldorff told the site at the Ocarina of Time's launch event in New York City. "There are fans of every single IP that we have out there. Of course, having new games in those series is wonderful, and I look forward to them as much as anyone else does, but there’s also a deep satisfaction in revisiting games that were very, very special, like Ocarina of Time… But it's also important to think about how many people had never played the original, and for them, the remake of Ocarina of Time is going to be an absolutely brand-new, 2026 experience, and one that I just cannot wait for them to get their hands on."

There's more interesting stuff in the interview, as Bihldorff outlines his views on the strenght of the Nintendo roster - "it doesn't matter how excited I am about Donkey Kong Bananza at launch; there's always going to be more games that are coming down the pipeline" - and that the release pipeline continues to look as strong for the Switch 2 as it did for the Switch. "There's one constant that has been consistent through my entire career at Nintendo, and that's that you can pretty much set your watch by the idea that we're going to be coming out with stuff," Bihldorff told Polygon.

Ocarina of Time is off to a very strong start; aside from being critically adored, the game has taken off virally - I can't move on my own feeds for clips of the game, people reminiscing about their original memories of certain locations, or long posts about the nostalgic elements of the title. Star Fox, meanwhile, has 1.17 million copies worldwide since its launch earlier this year on the Nintendo Switch 2, making it the ninth best-selling game on the platform (this is via Nintendo's financials yesterday). I expect Ocarina will outpace that.

Whatever your personal opinon on remakes in games, you cannot deny that it is a large part of the industry - and it seems Nintendo is keen to ride that wave as far as it'll go.

With all that said, when will I get my Pokemon Black and White remakes, then?

#3977. Swarmbreaker is an uncommonly mesmerising tower defence game in which enemies "cluster, collide and flow like a fluid"

It is said that King Canute once placed his throne on the shore and commanded the sea not to get his feet wet, thus proving to his flattering courtiers that only God Almighty holds sway over the elements. "But sire!" I would have told him, if I'd been one of the aforesaid lickspittles. "Why not lay down spike strips and park a couple of flamethrowers in the shallows?" I would have said this because I have just been playing Swarmbreaker, a tower defence game that aims to prove there is no fluid body so awe-inspiring that it cannot be machine-gunned into submission.

In Swarmbreaker - which launches on Steam tomorrow, and still has a demo as of writing – you have to defend your rocketship against waves of insect aggressors, who spawn at the map's far corners. Between waves, you spend earnings from kills on turrets, barricades, troops, and upgrades for all the foregoing. Sounds like bog-standard attrition management, perhaps, but what lifts Swarmbreaker is the "swarm" part. The rapacious scuttlers come in several distinct varieties, but they also "cluster, collide and flow like a fluid".

The results are hypnotic: coloured particles burst from each burrow and course through the map's contours, pushing movable terrain elements and eroding your structures like acid. You can practically hear the oil derricks fizz as they are engulfed and chewed to a lumpy puddle of iridescent digestive enzymes. Speaking of which, the more oil derricks you save during each wave, the more cash you'll have to spend before the next, but committing to their protection obviously risks leaving your ship exposed. Your fallback option is an inexhaustible mouse-click-fired artillery cannon, but this won't save you if the bulk of the swarm makes it all the way to your doorstep.

I'm still not convinced this isn't a run-of-the-mill tower defender, beneath it all, but it's worth giving the demo a shot just to enjoy the swirling tidal dynamics of homocidal buglife. What would King Canute have made of it all? I think he would have stuck his throne right by the biggest burrow, surrounded by gravity traps and howitzers. "Back in your hole, hungry liquids!" he'd have bellowed, firing dual AK47s simultaneously. "The only god I recognise is efficient chokepoint management! Death to sense-of-flow! Death to trickle-down politics!"

"SIRE," I'd have told him sternly. "You are getting your metaphors confused. And also that is a total waste of howitzers - those things are best placed on hills." Read more on Steam.
